#2751. Messer accounts for 4 TD as Florida Atlantic flies past UTSA, 60-29

Last time Florida Atlantic won six games in a season, the 2020s hadn't even begun. The year was 2019. Lane Kiffin was head coach. And the Owls were still members of Conference USA.

In year two of the Zach Kittley era, that coveted threshold was finally reached. Florida Atlantic secured bowl eligibility with its sixth victory of the season, and it could not have come in more emphatic fashion. The Owls overwhelmed UTSA, which entered the game boasting the American Conference's best overall record at 7-1, in a 60-29 offensive showcase Thursday night.

It marked the fourth 60-point performance in Florida Atlantic history and its second of the season, as the Owls out-gained the red-hot Roadrunners, 563-419.

Wide receiver Easton Messer continued to strengthen his All-American résumé. One week after catching all 16 passes thrown his way for 189 yards and three touchdowns, the receiver delivered another spectacular showing. The nation's receptions leader accounted for Florida Atlantic's first three touchdowns to construct a 21-7 advantage, which included two touchdown receptions and one touchdown pass. That early 14-point lead ensured Florida Atlantic would remain at least one step ahead of the Roadrunners for the remainder of the contest.

Messer's versatility was on full display Thursday. He finished with seven receptions for 85 yards and three touchdowns, added a 14-yard touchdown pass, and chipped in 34 punt return yards and eight rushing yards.

Messer became the first player to record three receiving touchdowns and a passing touchdown in a game since former Washington wide receiver Dante Pettis accomplished the feat in 2016. Over his last three games, Messer has accounted for 12 total touchdowns: eight receiving, two rushing, one passing, and one on a punt return.

His distributor, former Western Kentucky teammate, and best friend Caden Veltkamp may not have filled up the stat sheet to his usual extent, but the star quarterback delivered a remarkably efficient performance. Veltkamp attempted fewer than 30 passes against an FBS opponent for the first time this season, completing 17-of-25 throws for 210 yards and four touchdowns without an interception.

One week ago, Veltkamp attempted 56 passes, tied for the most by any FBS quarterback this season. This time, the air raid offense received its best run support of the season. Florida Atlantic entered the matchup ranked 121st nationally in rushing offense, averaging just 110 yards per game. But against UTSA, the Owls exploded for 339 yards on the ground.

Leonard Farrow captained the attack with a season-high 126 rushing yards, punctuated by a 59-yard touchdown in the late third quarter to extend the lead to 50-29. Ethan Ervin contributed 92 yards, while Kaden Shields-Dutton added 45 yards, as Florida Atlantic repeatedly gashed UTSA for explosive gains.

Florida Atlantic had yet to establish a rushing attack of that magnitude all season, but the offensive fireworks were nothing new for the Owls. The difference Thursday night was what transpired on the opposite side of the ball. Florida Atlantic allowed at least 48 points in each of its last three outings, but the defense brought a different intensity against UTSA.

First, the Owls won the turnover battle 2-0, with Deshaun Batiste and Joseph Sipp Jr. recovering fumbles that were converted into 11 points. Additionally, the Owls thoroughly dominated UTSA's offensive line. Roadrunners quarterback Owen McCown still managed 265 passing yards and three touchdowns, he spent much of the evening under duress. Florida Atlantic repeatedly collapsed the pocket, registering six sacks and 11 tackles for loss. TCU transfer Jonathan Bax spearheaded the effort with a team-high 2.5 sacks.

When Florida Atlantic had a brief offensive lull in the third quarter, the defense stepped up to ensure there would be no UTSA comeback, forcing consecutive punts while the Owls held onto a 43-29 lead. The unit was particularly stingy on third down, limiting the Roadrunners to a 5-of-16 showing.

With both sides of the ball coming together, Florida Atlantic engineered its strongest performance of the season, knocking off UTSA as a touchdown underdog. The Owls improved to 5-0 at home for the first time in program history, with only a Nov. 21 showdown against South Florida standing between them and an unblemished record in Boca Raton.

UTSA (7-2, 4-1 American) suffered its first conference defeat of the season, becoming the last American team to accrue its second overall loss. The Roadrunners entered Thursday sitting just three spots outside the AP Top 25, but their College Football Playoff aspirations took a significant blow in Boca Raton. The defeat also marked UTSA's first loss to Florida Atlantic since 2020.

Florida Atlantic (6-3, 3-2 American) secured bowl eligibility for the first time since 2020 and reached the six-win mark for the first time since 2019. The Owls have averaged 50.7 points per game over their last three outings, signaling that Kittley's offense has hit its stride. But another dimension was added Thursday. Against one of the American's premier contenders, Florida Atlantic showed a glimpse of its potential when the defense matches the firepower of its offense.

Veteran WR Brandon Aiyuk owes the 49ers roughly $13 million in bonus forfeiture — a potential complication in his efforts to secure his release by reporting to the facility Friday.

The NFL Management Council and the NFL Players Association are both involved in attempting to resolve the situation. The sides could reach an agreement to pay back the money, or it could go to arbitration. But it's complicated and may take time to resolve.

The more fascinating aspect is what happens with Aiyuk's contract. Currently, Aiyuk's under contract through 2028. If he agrees to a restructured contract, likely one that makes him a free agent at the end of the season, why would the Niners part ways with him?

The answer would be that both sides believe they have reached a point of no return; there are no actions left to take, and it's best to part ways with Aiyuk.

You could also include Aiyuk in any potential trade—even as a throw-in in place of a draft pick. You might ask why a team would take a risk on a player who hasn't stepped foot on an NFL field in over two seasons.

After it's all said and done, there's a plausible outcome where Aiyuk remains on the roster — whether he suits up is another question.

But if you're Kyle Shanahan and you're looking at a wide receiver depth chart without Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, potentially Christian Kirk, and another month-plus without De'Zhaun Stribling, you'd think it'd be easy to swallow your pride and take Aiyuk back — provided the locker room does.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2747. What we learned from the Spurs win over the Mavericks

At some point between the end of the '21 season and the start of the '22 season, I made a pact with myself: no more first quarters.

You have to understand, these were dark times to be a Spurs writer.

And yes, I know, as a fan myself, that those years were no more of picnic for the average fan than they were for me, but still. There's just something about watching a beating and then having to write about it that feels vaguely abusive, especially when some of your favorite people are still involved.

Having to watch Gregg Popovich lose like that…I felt like a journalist covering Muhammad Ali's last fights.

It didn't matter how valiant he was, how much he tried to make something out of nothing — it just seemed kind of dirty to watch at all. We all knew what he was doing, of course.

But watching a worthy sacrifice doesn't make it any easier. I still get misty-eyed when the Iron Giant tells Hogarth Hughes not to follow him (as if he could) before rocketing from the ground into space, and meeting the falling arc of a nuclear warhead.

There's a reason I don't watch the movie all the time. It would be fairly masochistic of me to do so.

But there are 82 games in a season, and someone has to cover them.

As a writing staff, you take some solace in the knowledge that you're all in this together. You're all having to write about it. You're all having to dig for silver linings. And that (for this site) you're all doing it out of some (possibly misplaced) sense of love for the team, and the sport, and the readers who are just about as miserable as you are.

But I just could not watch first quarters anymore. Not in real time.

It's one thing to know that the Titanic is sinking; to be thrown into the middle of the chaos and do your best to make sense of it. It's another thing altogether to watch the ship headed towards the ice-burg in the darkness. To hear the godawful scraping and know what it means. To have been watching the journey for years, and completely run out of ways to spin it.

It had to have been a very conscious decision on James Cameron's part to make that movie a romance. How else could you get people to watch it? The wreck just cannot be the main course.

I couldn't convince myself to watch the game at all if I started with the first quarter. The Spurs would either start taking their beating from the onset, or worse, soar to an early lead that we all knew wouldn't last.

So I decided that I would start watching during the second quarter, finish the game, and then watch the beginning.

It was so much easier to bear when you already knew how it would end. Especially when the Spurs did miraculously pull off the win.

You could go back and break down how the positive momentum started, with the empty but understandable hope that there might be something algorithmic in those 12 minutes that could be reverse-engineered and employed more regularly.

And even the sting of defeat didn't smart as much when you were able to initially avoid the fool's gold of productive opening minutes.

Hell, sometimes it was even a little funny when you encountered the Spurs finding a way to lose the opening frame that you'd never even considered.

(Even though the Spurs won the game, I don't think I'll ever forget Jakob Poeltl picking up 2 fouls in the first 96 seconds of the Lakers game in 2022 that tied Pop with Don Nelson.)

Lately, though, I've been forced to reconsider my first-quarter policy, and the reason is pretty obvious: Victor Wembanyama is just too fun to be put on the back-burner in any capacity.

It was a sensible policy when the losses were piling up. Sometimes it still is.

But frustration with a contender-caliber team starting slowly is simply not enough to deprive myself of the immediacy of the joy provided by the most insane fusion of Hakeem Olajuwon, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Wilt Chamberlain imaginable.

Wemby just had the first *official* 50 point, 20 rebound, 8 block game in NBA history (and the first 50/20/10 in the non-assist category if you combine his steals and blocks), in his 8th game of his 4th season, and he's the same age that Wilt was as a rookie!

Chamberlain didn't even peak until he was 25!

That's the territory we're in. That's the conversation.

And that's in spite of existing in the era of injury and rest management. In spite of the fact that Wemby's doing it on a team that's good enough to have already made the Finals.

In spite of playing in an era where blocks are harder to come by, and strategic scouting and game-plans are another level, and players are (pretty successfully) bombing away from long range. In spite of an out-of-whack jumper that's converting at about 28% outside of 10 feet.

Having chugged a 16oz energy drink during my late dinner before the game in an attempt to battle the somnolent rigidities of middle-age, I found myself doing the same 'fighting the urge to pee' dance that my child still breaks out every now and then, as I tried to hold out til the end of the half.

Smelling weakness through the television screen like a shark loose in a blood bank, Wemby proceeded to block three shots in roughly 13 seconds, as if to say: are you sure that you want to miss this?

I can't remember the last time I almost wet myself over basketball, or a more satisfying pee at the half.

There's plenty of negative things I could say about the game. I don't know that I've ever seen this team shoot that badly as a whole. Even Julian Champagnie and Devin Vassell couldn't buy a shot.

There's no reason it should have been that close with such a performance out of Wembanyama.

The bench's defense looked like it had been coordinated by Wile E. Coyote and the Acme Corporation, and they put up a total of ten points in their relief of the starters. Carter Bryant and Tarris Reed somehow got no minutes on a night in which it couldn't have been more clear that a shakeup was needed.

Even De'Aaron Fox's previously next-level show of efficiency took the wrong turn at Albuquerque.

This was a bad game, if we're being honest. A real stinker. And yet I can't find the animosity within me to make this the all-around feel-bad roast that it should be, because, as I've said so many times over the last year, it just did not matter.

This should have been one of those games where I had to go back and break down the first quarter in a state of rage.

It should have been. But I just don't have it in me to despair the undespairing.

Through it all, Wemby was completely unshaken. Understandably, so were his teammates. In their shoes, I think I'd feel the same way.

I don't love that they frittered away lead after lead. I don't like it as a trend, and I don't like it as reminder.

But I think it's easy to forget that we don't live in that place were I can't stand to watch the first quarter anymore, and that by resigning myself to that policy of the past, I'd be getting in the way of my own happiness.

You can't protect yourself from pain without also protecting yourself from rapture. I think sometimes, in both life and basketball, we have a way of forgetting that.

I can tell you everything they did wrong. I can rant and rage with the best of them, and sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.

I can tell you that they were saved anyway, undeservingly.

Give me a better story than that, I dare you.

I don't have a lot of nice things to say about this game, but man has Wemby really taken to the responsibility of attacking the rim this season. Right now he and Giannis are the only players in the NBA averaging 7+ Rim FGs and 8+ Paint FGs made per game. And Wemby's actually doing it more ways than Giannis is, as the only player in the league averaging 5+ points as the P&R Roll Man, 4+ Points off of Cuts, and 4+ points In Transition, per game. If his jumper starts heating up, we're going to see even crazier numbers than we did last night. Which is insane when you consider that he's 4th in the league in scoring with a jumper finds the bottom of the bucket about 1/4th of time right now.

It's been a bit of an uncomfortable fit for Stephon Castle when all three guards are on the court at the same time, and he seems to have been asked to serve as more of an off-ball shooter because of that, but when the need arises, he always seems to find an extra gear. I know many are hoping that the addition of Tobias Harris forces some rotation adjustments, but I will say, Castle is getting the open shots, and he's not shrinking from the challenge. He's shooting 32% from three now, but if he starts hitting those, that lineup might really morph into something scary, because everything will open up on the inside, and Wemby's already mutilating the rim as it is (and Harper's been slouch, either). And as much as I think Harris will be a boon to the team, I'd secretly prefer to see that happen instead.

Though Fox had probably his most inefficient night of the season on the offensive end, he's still the only player in the NBA creating 15+ Assist Points Per Game, with a 2-1 Assist-to-Turnover Ratio, while also sporting a 65+ True Shooting Percentage, which is crazy when you see all the names that miss the mark. But, just as importantly, he's been outstanding on the defensive end, and it showed in the clutch last night when he kept the still-lethal (and long-time Spurs killer) Kyrie Irving off-balance just enough to that his attempt at a game-winning bucket. To have lost a game with Victor playing like that would have felt catastrophic, so he'd be next in line for the game ball, in my mind.

#2746. Will Arch Manning, Dante Moore and other QB prospect questions influence NFL trade deadline?

As Tuesday's NFL trade deadline draws closer, front offices at all 32 teams are asking themselves: How much do we value our coming draft picks?

And how does that value compare to our assessment of this year's trade candidates?

The question circulates every year. But with a 2027 NFL Draft class that was strongly heralded in the spring, the calculus feels different.

"Last year, the '27 draft was looming over the '26 draft far more than usual," said a league source with a long history of evaluating the NFL Draft and its quarterback landscape, speaking on condition of anonymity in order to speak freely. "And it has not been a stellar year."

In particular, the first half of the 2026 college football season has not raised the NFL's excitement level about the quarterback class that awaits. Fair or not, that buzz tends to influence the perception of the entire class.

So while talent evaluations between now and April could still shift, it's worth asking: Will a shift in perception of the coming quarterback class influence the NFL trade deadline next week?

Texas QB Arch Manning has cast doubt on his NFL draft potential with his inconsistent play for the Longhorns this season.

In April, teams were wary of trading away 2027 picks due to the buzz around the class, which stemmed largely from buzz around the crop of potential first-round quarterbacks. If the hype has dimmed, are those picks more for sale?

Like most trends in the NFL, the philosophy will differ from team to team. But conversations with league and team voices acknowledge that some draft-eligible players are losing their shine, and some teams could parlay that belief into feeling emboldened at the deadline to acquire players at positions they may not feel the draft is guaranteed to deliver.

Information on draft prospects is incomplete by early November. But one high-ranking AFC executive said they could already get a general sense of the deeper and shallower areas of the draft even if individual evaluations remain unfinished.

"You have all the information, you have general medical history and then you have early background and you can kind of form [opinions]," one high-ranking AFC executive told Yahoo Sports. "You can get close enough to where it's like, 'OK, it's deep. We can solve that in the draft.' Or you're blending with the draft from free agency where it's like [a position] is weaker than other years based on our information [so] it probably makes sense to make this move because between now and the draft, we probably can't solve it the way we want to solve it if we don't do this.

"You're trying to use all that information to piece together the plan."

What information will teams across the league be piecing together? Here's what Yahoo Sports is hearing.

Conversations with executives and evaluators across six different teams offered a mosaic of opinions.

Evaluators from two AFC teams and a high-ranking executive from an NFC team each confirmed they do not view the 2027 NFL Draft as highly now as they did this summer. Each said that reflected their current evaluations of the quarterback class.

"I was part of [the hype], too," one AFC evaluator said. "I got caught up, probably told a bunch of people how this is going to be one of the best draft classes in a long time and it's turning out [not] to be. … There's some good players and there's some really good players at the top, like [Ohio State receiver] Jeremiah Smith. There's a few other players that are really, really talented, but they have a lot of baggage. …

"But this draft isn't turning out to be as deep and as loaded as I anticipated and hoped."

The evaluator from the other AFC team said they believe that 75-80% of draft classes are similarly talented, but perceptions of elite players at premium positions — quarterback, receiver, edge rusher and offensive tackle — disproportionately shift perceptions of each draft. This year, the evaluator saw a dip in receiver, edge and quarterback certainty.

"If that's the case, it's worth buying a player that you can get control on rather than waiting and guessing at the draft," an NFC executive said. "I do think that's part of the Texans' thesis with Marvin Harrison."

Quarterback questions from evaluators rage: Is Mississippi's 6-foot Trinidad Chambliss big enough for the league? Will Miami's Darian Mensah have faced tough enough defenses to predict his pro success accurately? Are college defensive coordinators overwhelmingly cracking the code on college quarterbacks more effectively?

The two biggest question marks at quarterback this season stem from Texas quarterback Arch Manning and Oregon quarterback Dante Moore. Manning has proven inconsistent through eight games, including in pivotal moments. Moore's season ended Sept. 26 after he suffered a concussion. Questions on each player weigh their readiness for the NFL and their interest in declaring pro this spring rather than exploring another college year.

Evaluators are split on whether a transfer would help Manning find a better offensive fit. One camp believes that would be the fresh start he needs, while the other believes his family pedigree and résumé will already net him first-round consideration so having just one year to adjust to a new system alongside new teammates could end up hurting his stock more than helping it. Moore, meanwhile, could help his stock if he shows a cleaner bill of health and gets more than his current limited sample size of 19 college starts, evaluators said.

Several quarterbacks are still expected to be drafted in the first round, including the season's biggest riser to this point in Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker. One AFC evaluator said Mestemaker, Notre Dame's CJ Carr and Mensah each would have earned higher evaluations than 2026 first overall pick Fernando Mendoza. Chambliss and Missouri's Austin Simmons intrigue evaluators as well.

Even with mixed reviews on premium positions, including quarterback, a high-ranking AFC executive and a high-ranking NFC executive agreed the draft has more consensus high-end talent than the 2026 class.

"I would say this [year] is maybe a little deeper than last year's in the top 15-20 picks in other positions than quarterback," the high-ranking NFC executive said. "But then after that, it seems like it's a little leaner, and the drafts have been getting a little leaner."

The high-ranking AFC executive credited last year's offensive tackle class and a handful of elite players, like Giants linebacker Arvell Reese. The executive wondered: Are quarterbacks shifting the perception too much?

"The quarterback class, I think people just keep overcorrecting," the executive said. "I think they overcorrected high and now they're overcorrecting all these guys can't play, they'll all stay in school.

"A lot of the sentiment on the draft is driven by what people think about the QBs. But I think even if you take them out, there's some really, really high-end dudes in this draft."

Evaluators and executives were split on how much the coming draft truly influences teams' trade deadline strategies.

Some evaluators and executives emphasized building a roster is a holistic process that constantly requires a multiyear vision integrating the trade deadline, free agency and draft.

Others believed trade-deadline acquisitions, and their often steep costs, prioritize the current season's outlook. A league source considered teams in three categories.

"There's a team that they're not going to get in the playoffs and so they're doing the best they can to build a winning culture and they're basically playing for next year," the source said of the first group. "Then you have a group of teams that they can get in the playoffs, but they can't win in the playoffs. …

"Then you get teams [that], hey, get in the playoffs and anything can happen."

Expect teams like the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs and Chicago Bears (Jeffery Simmons already, but perhaps more?) to buy, capitalizing on their already-high ceilings.

Expect teams like the Minnesota Vikings, Pittsburgh Steelers and Seattle Seahawks (like the Bears, they've already started) to assess whether they can narrow the gap on rosters that simultaneously hold glaring weaknesses and playoff-caliber strengths.

And then expect teams like the Indianapolis Colts (in progress), Tennessee Titans (in progress, via Simmons trade) and perhaps even the Las Vegas Raiders to recognize that accumulating assets for next year and beyond is more valuable.

That trifecta should guide teams making bigger swings, the league source said. A high-ranking AFC executive believed there was more nuance involved.

"Honestly, every team in each segment has an argument to make a trade," the executive said. "It's just the level."

Players with potential to meaningfully impact a team beyond 2026 could attract suitors from different competitive stages. Expensive players at depreciating positions (looking at you, Jonathan Taylor) make less sense for teams that aren't contending this season.

Whether teams have a scarcity mindset around draft picks could unfold similarly: Teams like the Titans, New York Jets and Los Angeles Chargers would have little reason to send off their first-round pick as they struggle to win games. But sending a mid-round pick for a player on an expiring deal? Those decisions are more record- and draft class-agnostic, some believe.

"I don't think people care when they trade a third or a fourth," an AFC talent evaluator said. "They look at those as pretty stable resources year over year.

"But I think the teams maybe that are at the top of the draft would maybe consider it because you can kind of anticipate those spots by what's going to be available."

Arguably the most important caveat in any of these decisions: accurately assessing a team's place in its competitive and resource-allocation lifecycle. Trades bust most when teams overestimate their readiness, as the Colts did last year when trading two first-round picks for cornerback Sauce Gardner and the Atlanta Falcons traded back into the first round of the 2025 NFL Draft for edge rusher James Pearce Jr. In contrast, a Bears team that won two of three games even without Caleb Williams this year gave counterparts more confidence in its logic to send two first-rounders for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.

"The teams that do the best job on these trades [are] really understanding what phase you're in and stacking it," the AFC talent evaluator said. "Seattle has a loaded roster and one elite guard really helped them. The Jets have tons of draft capital so acquiring picks makes sense. When you cherry-pick and only do one here and there, I don't think you really get the value or help your franchise long term.

"It's really just a constant balance and a constant push and pull of trying to identify where your team is and what you're going to be in a year or two years because that's where it becomes really valuable."

#2742. Things aren't unfolding how Aaron Donald and the Rams envisioned, but he's here and enjoying it

WOODLAND HILLS, Calif. –– A particular kind of silence follows a legend's return.

Narratives write themselves in advance — the final act, the curtain call, the one last ride where the old king straps on the armor and reminds everyone why the kingdom still bears his name.

We, the witnesses, are greedy for that story. We want the coronation. We script it before the first snap and then get offended when reality refuses to read the script.

Aaron Donald has spent half a season watching reality refuse to read the script.

He came back — unretired, un-dusted, un-done — to headline a defense that was supposed to be the counterweight to a star-laden offense.

He came back to play beside Myles Garrett, the man who dropped 22.5 sacks on the league last season, to play with Trent McDuffie and a secondary built like a bank vault.

Donald came back because the vision was beautiful: Donald and Garrett collapsing pockets, the back end locking receivers in a trunk, the whole machine humming, while Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua and the rest of the fireworks show did their thing on the other side of the ball.

None of it unfolded the way he thought it would.

"I don't got to go into detail as far as that," Donald said.

Something in the way he said it—the shrug in his voice, the laugh hiding underneath—told you the details don't wound him anymore.

"But no, it's not what I expected, but we here. And I'm going to enjoy it though, you know. I'm enjoying the process. I'm enjoying myself week in and week out getting better. I'm enjoying being out there with the guys," Donald said.

There's the headline hiding in plain sight. The man who spent nine years snarling at quarterbacks and answering reporters in clipped, guarded sentences is — at 35, with hands that hurt and a body that aches like a weather report — suddenly the most quotable man in the building.

"You seem a little bit looser than maybe the first time we covered you," a reporter observed, and Donald didn't deny it.

"Maybe I just didn't want to talk to y'all or something. I don't know. Maybe I miss y'all. That's probably what it is, huh," Donald said. "I'm just having fun, man. That's it. Thirty-five years old playing football. It's a kids' game."

Aaron Donald — the most terrifying interior defender of his generation, a man who treated offensive lines like speed bumps — calling football a kids' game with the affection of a father watching from a folding chair.

His fire hasn't gone out; it's just stopped burning him alive.

Something happens to great players when the end comes into view––urgency relaxes into gratitude. The grind becomes the gift.

Donald isn't chasing legacy anymore; legacy is chained to his ankle whether he runs or not.

What's left is the Sunday itself — the pads, the smell, the snap, the small daily miracle that a body held together by tape and stubbornness still answers the bell.

"Ain't what I expected, but I'm enjoying it," Donald said.

If you want to understand the new Aaron Donald, start with Justin Herbert's fumble.

Last week against the Chargers, Wesley Bailey pried the ball loose, and there it was — a defensive tackle's fever dream, a scoop-and-score with nothing but green grass and glory ahead.

Donald's older brother called him afterward: "Man, how you missed your touchdown? We've been talking about that," Donald said.

His retelling of the moment is pure cinema, the kind of story only a man at peace with himself tells on himself this hard.

"I seen a ball. First thing came to my head — touchdown. I'm going to get this ball. I should have slowed down, but I felt people behind me like, I don't want to get hit in my back. That's going to hurt. So I tried to go full speed and scoop it. The ball was going — I thought the ball was going to bounce this way, but it bounced that way. And it just looked all damn silly. And then I hit the ball out and I just laid there. I can't believe I just did that," Donald said.

He lay on the turf, a three-time Defensive Player of the Year, flat on his back, smiling at the heavens, mourning a touchdown that existed only in his imagination.

Stafford, mic'd up, could be heard sympathizing: People don't realize how challenging it is at their age to bend over and get a ball.

Sean McVay texted him that night to joke about it.

"You know, a lot of guys joked about it, and to be honest, I was a little upset with it, you know, because it could have put some more points on the board, at least got the ball back for the offense in the short field. But it's all fun and games because we won. If it was a different situation and we didn't win, it'd be a lot worse," Donald said.

And then, the detail that tells you everything: Donald was at the front of the line during scoop drills this week.

Three Defensive Player of the Year trophies on his shelf, and he's practicing picking up a bouncing football like a rookie trying to make the roster.

"That was my — I needed that. I need that. Learning bending, getting down. So when opportunity presents itself again, I take advantage of it."

Now for the part that stings. Because the vision was never just Donald. The vision was Donald and Garrett — two of the most destructive pass rushers breathing, sharing the same line, splitting the same blocking schemes, forcing offenses to pick their poison and find out both cups are poisoned.

Garrett has been sidelined since Week 1, and the defense Donald came back to anchor has been assembling itself in real time, week by week, like a man rebuilding an engine in his driveway.

The Rams stumbled to a 4-4 start precisely because the grand design kept tearing at the seams.

So when Garrett returned to practice this week, you could hear the exhale across the entire facility.

"It's good to have the pieces back to the puzzle," Donald said. "Was good to see him out there yesterday, today looking good, looking fast. Getting to work with them in full pads and playing off each other — looked pretty good today. I'm excited about having him here, having him back obviously and seeing what he does Sunday."

Jayden Daniels — a mobile quarterback in a season where mobile quarterbacks have been a problem, Josh Allen rumbling for 100-plus rushing yards against this defense a few weeks back, Daniels himself topping 100 against the Giants earlier in the year.

"We got a good game plan. We've been talking about it. Cleaning up some things up front that we can do better — playing off each other, I should say — to not allow him to gash us and hurt us. I'm pretty sure he's going to get a couple plays here and there, but as long as we kind of keep him contained, keep him in the pocket, not let him get them big rush lanes where he can just take advantage of, we'll be fine," Donald said.

The math is delicious, and Donald knows it.

If Garrett is finally, truly back — and "the guy did have 20-something sacks last year," as Donald reminded everyone — then offenses can no longer tilt the entire map toward No. 99. The double-teams have to divide. The protection schemes have to choose a death.

There are a million ways to die; offenses must pick their poison.

"If Miles is 100% ready to go and he plays this week, that's going to be amazing for us. Because it's always good when you got all the pieces to the puzzle out there," Donald said.

The crowning jewel, arriving fashionably late to his own coronation.

Lost in the Garrett noise is what Donald sees behind him — and what he sees, he trusts.

The Rams lost Jaylen Watson for the season with a shoulder injury.

Emmanuel Forbes is stepping into the vacancy.

And when I asked Donald whether he's ever played with a secondary of this caliber — Trent McDuffie, Kam Kitchens and Quentin Lake — he didn't hesitate.

"I played with some good guys, but there's been some playmakers back there that's playing some good ball right now. And obviously when you lose a good player, you got another guy to step up that you trust, and it's always next man up, right? Understanding that the guy that's going to step in, it's not going to be too big of a drop off," Donald said.

Then he reached back, and you could hear the nostalgia braid itself into the present tense.

"It feels good when you got guys on the back end that you can trust. I had some years where I played with some really good football players that played on the back end, where you knew they'd be able to hold the ball a little longer and you get some opportunities to get after the quarterback. And it's like it feels like that again."

Donald doesn't name those years. He doesn't have to.

Every Rams fan who watched the Super Bowl run knows exactly which secondary he's conjuring — the one that let the front four hunt a half-second longer, the one that turned coverage sacks into game-turning plays.

"I think it can be fun. So I'm excited about it. Just ready to go out there and play some ball," Donald said.

Donald won't say everything. That's the tacenda of this season — the unspoken ledger every great player keeps when the plan collapses, and the world starts writing obituaries at 2-4.

He could catalog the injuries, the broken rotations, the games that got away. He chooses not to. Not because the wounds aren't real but because airing them changes nothing, and Aaron Donald has never once confused complaining with competing.

Asked why adversity matters at 4-4, he gave the answer of a man who has stopped negotiating with circumstances.

"There's no way to avoid it. It's going to be ups and downs in a football season. It just happened to happen early. Like I said before, it was nothing to panic about. We just got to keep playing good ball week in and week out, trying to find ways to stay together. Even though the outside world saying whatever they saying, as long as we stay connected inside and we just continue to work through the adversity — because there's no way you can go around it, it's just a part of the game," Donald said.

Stay connected inside; let the outside world talk.

It's the oldest wisdom in football, and it sounds different coming from him now — less like a slogan, more like a man describing how he survived his own expectations.

Because that's the real story here. Not the record. Not the injuries. The metamorphosis. The snarling interior menace of the McVay era has become something rarer and more compelling: a veteran who has made peace with the gap between the vision and the reality, who practices scoop drills at the front of the line, who jokes with reporters he once treated like intruders, who calls a brutal, aching, 35-year-old season a gift.

"You know, from the beginning, nothing played out how I thought it was," Donald said. "You got your vision, you kind of think what can happen. It's like it was a whole 360 of how everything played out for me."

The circle, closing. The man who came back for a coronation discovered the season wasn't about the crown at all — it was about the company. The puzzle, slowly reassembling itself. Garrett on one edge, Donald on the interior, a trusted secondary behind them and a quarterback on Sunday who will find out, probably the hard way, what this defense looks like when the pieces finally all stand in the same frame at once.

"It's never going to be what you expected," Donald said.

Sunday in Washington, the expectation finally matches the reality. For the first time all season, Aaron Donald gets to share a field with Myles Garrett — and if you're Jayden Daniels, reading that sentence should ruin your weekend.

#2739. Jones - the smiling wind-up artist who refuses to fade away

An Eddie Jones press conference has always been an event in itself.

You never quite know what is coming. A compliment, a cutting observation, a verbal grenade. Sometimes all three, invariably delivered with that mischievous smile.

Jones belongs to a disappearing generation of coaches who understood that the contest could begin long before the players took the field.

Warren Gatland could intimidate with his imposing presence and gruff demeanour alone. Jose Mourinho proclaimed himself 'The Special One' and made confrontation an art form.

Jones was different. Small in stature, with an almost permanent grin, he could stir up an entire nation while thoroughly enjoying himself.

All three built reputations on dominance. Not simply on the pitch, but over the agenda, their players and the organisations they represented.

But the language of coaching is changing.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy talks about connection and relationships. Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler emphasises collaboration, trust and understanding the person behind the player.

Neither lacks ambition or authority, but their approach contrasts with the era of the all-powerful head coach.

At 66, Jones remains one of rugby's most fascinating characters from that old school.

In 2018 Jones questioned whether Wales fly-half Rhys Patchell could handle the pressure of playing England at Twickenham, while describing Warren Gatland's team as "confident and cocky".

But his provocations sometimes crossed the line.

That same year Jones apologised after footage emerged of him using some choice language to describe Wales and Ireland in less than flattering terms at a sponsor's event the previous year.

The former was classic Jones. Identify a weakness, plant a seed of doubt and ensure everyone was talking about it. The latter showed when the wind-ups went too far.

Speaking to BBC Sport prior to Japan's Nations Championship meeting with Wales, Jones offered an intriguing explanation.

"Some of them were planned to an extent. Others might have come out of the press conference. Sometimes you say things at the press conference that you don't mean to say. But, yeah, sometimes."

Players picked on form not club location - Tandy

Jones looks to create Japan history in Cardiff

"And particularly with England, I always felt with the English that they didn't have enough confidence in themselves."

Jones explained that part of his responsibility was to provide that self-belief.

"So I felt one of my roles was to give them that confidence, to be almost the battering ram for them."

For Jones, the mind games served more than one purpose. Unsettling opponents was one thing, but taking pressure off his players was just as important.

And if that meant making himself the centre of attention, so be it.

An extraordinary workaholic, he is renowned for his almost impossible standards. Players have described receiving messages from him at 3am while he was exercising, only to be questioned at breakfast about why they had not replied.

Yet even as an international coach, Jones has been known to quietly turn up at local clubs to coach minis, or drive hours to a player's testimonial dinner without a fee.

His career has had its extremes. England dismissed him in 2022, while his return to Australia ended with the Wallabies' first pool-stage exit at the 2023 World Cup.

In Lyon, after Australia had been thrashed by Wales, the familiar grin was absent. Jones was prickly, irritated and facing questions about his future.

Three years on, as he looked forward to Japan facing Wales in Cardiff in the Nations Championship on Saturday, the contrast was striking. Relaxed, charming and generous with his answers, he appeared to be thoroughly enjoying himself.

Born in Australia with a Japanese mother, Eddie Jones has had two spells as Japan head coach [Getty Images]

For all his contradictions, Jones remains a rugby obsessive. Nothing illustrated that better than his answer when asked which Welsh player had left the greatest impression on him.

Not Gareth Edwards, Shane Williams or Alun Wyn Jones, but Liam Williams, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions full-back renowned for his bravery under the high ball.

"Every time I come to Millennium Stadium (sic), I have this picture of Liam Williams winning box kicks," Jones told the Scrum V podcast.

"He was all elbows and knees, but he could do something brilliant in the game."

It was a rugby purist's answer. An appreciation of the finer details rather than simply the most celebrated names.

That affection for the finer details extends to Welsh rugby more broadly.

Jones spoke warmly of Cardiff's Principality Stadium and praised Steve Tandy's rebuilding work, particularly the leadership of Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan.

But the old competitive instincts remain.

Japan's coach knows the value of silencing the Cardiff crowd, and believes a strong start could turn Welsh supporters' frustrations into a psychological advantage.

Even the charming, reflective Jones is still searching for an edge.

As the conversation ended, he offered encouragement to Welsh supporters.

"So, yeah, for the Welsh supporters, just keep backing your team."

"But don't back them too much on Saturday."

Wales opt for centre power pair against Japan

#2734. Game Preview #10: Wolves at Pelicans Game Thread

Fresh off of a tough win against a talented Houston Rockets squad, the Minnesota Timberwolves take on Zion Williamson and the New Orleans Pelicans on Friday night.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (6-3) vs New Orleans Pelicans (4-4)

Where: Smoothie King Center — New Orleans, LA

After starting the year 0-4, the Pelicans have ripped off four straight wins to claw back to .500. Sprinkled into that winning streak are some impressive victories over the surging Memphis Grizzlies (handing them their only loss on the season thus far) and the Atlanta Hawks. New Orleans is not a squad that is projected to climb the Western Conference standings or necessarily strike fear in the hearts of opponents, though they are still a team with enough competitive and ascending players to keep opponents honest.

Considering the still shorthanded state of the Wolves, they may have their hands full with a healthy-for-now Pelicans team. The win over the Rockets was thoroughly impressive, though Chris Finch and company will need to remain focused if they are to come out of this game with a victory.

Here are a few things I am looking out for against New Orleans:

You know the guys – the dudes who love to turn up and have career games against the Wolves no matter what state their team is in. Most teams in the NBA have at least one Wolf Killer. The Pelicans have a few.

Perhaps most obvious of these players is Zion Williamson, who averages a whopping 28.5 points per game against Minnesota, nearly five points higher than his career average of 23.8. When healthy, Williamson is one of the premier tickets in the league and can score at will against nearly anyone. Jonathan Kuminga and Rudy Gobert will have their hands full with Zion, who will seek to outmuscle and overpower anyone that Finch decides to throw at him.

Saddiq Bey is another player that ramps up his production against the Timberwolves. A career 14.8 ppg scorer, his number increases to 19.5 for his career against Minnesota. As a member of the Pelicans, Bey's average jumps up to 24 ppg versus the Wolves. The guy just flat out doesn't like us.

As the Pelicans have other surging young players contributing to their recent run of success, this matchup may be more difficult than initially expected. Derik Queen has looked to be a solid NBA big man and Jeremiah Fears has been becoming a more well-rounded player. If Minnesota's defenders can keep the Wolf Killers from transforming into much better versions of themselves, the game is there for the taking.

Bones Hyland is a fun player. He's energetic, has a great smile, and keeps the fanbase engaged with his aesthetically pleasing style of play and affable three-point shot celebration. He's an ideal bench player that could fit in on many teams. We are fortunate to have him as a Timberwolf.

However, with a slew of injuries that continue to hamper Minnesota's preferred personnel, Bones continues to be thrust into heavier minutes than he would normally get. In the four games before Anthony Edwards got injured, Hyland played an average of eight minutes per night. Since then, his minutes have doubled, playing 16 minutes per game in the five matchups since Edwards (and now Terrence Shannon Jr.) went down.

Bones's 19 point, eight assist night against the Los Angeles Clippers last week was a true representation of what he can bring as a player when he's on. It's unrealistic to expect that kind of production and efficiency from him most nights, though he does help the Timberwolves find tempo and form whenever things are going south.

If the Timberwolves are going to have any sustained success while Edwards and TSJ are out, Hyland will need to continue to exert efficiency and production in his limited time on the court. He was electric against the Rockets, scoring 19 points in just 16 minutes of play. For a team that continues to lose players at a high clip, Bones will remain an integral part of the offensive flow moving forward.

There's not much more that can be said about just how putrid Minnesota's free throw shooting has been. Currently the team sits at 63.4%, good for dead last and a massive 7% behind the next closest team, which is the 1-7 Milwaukee Bucks. Minnesota shot a cool 53% (10-19) at the line just last night versus Houston in a 10-point victory to bring that percentage down even lower. So it goes.

It's not like this team has a problem shooting the ball, either. That's what makes this ineptitude so baffling. The Timberwolves shot 53% from the floor and 43% from distance against the Rockets. And yet, while standing at the free throw line, uncontested and still, they can't put the ball in the hoop.

Two players on the Wolves are shooting greater than 80% from the line this season. Everyone else is below them. That is unacceptable.

It would appear that Gobert's inability to consistently make shots from the charity stripe (42.6% on nearly six attempts per game) is becoming contagious to the rest of the team. While it hasn't been the biggest issue the Timberwolves have faced this season, it will become one as the team enters more late-game clutch time situations. We're not far off from a few tight losses spurring a dialogue that laments the team's lack of efficiency from the line. The recent defeat at the hands of the Golden State Warriors comes to mind, poor officiating be damned.

Chris Finch will need to address this problem somehow. Unfortunately, getting reps from the free throw line will not show itself as immediately game-changing. It will take time. Finishing this season anywhere but dead last should be seen as a success at this point. Until then, Minnesota needs to figure out how to capitalize on the opportunities they are given.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2731. 4 things to watch as the Mavericks’ Cup quest continues against the Utah Jazz

The Dallas Mavericks (4-4) will meet the Utah Jazz (1-7) 7:00pm CST Friday at American Airlines Center in the the group stage of the in-season NBA Cup tournament. Dallas enters this contest on a two-game slide after their comeback attempt Wednesday against San Antonio came up short, 112-111. After a challenging stretch of the schedule to begin the season, the Mavericks face their second opponent this week to bring a record with fewer than two wins into the AAC; Monday the Sacramento Kings improved to 1-6 against a Mavericks team without Kyrie Irving, 115-100. The Jazz arrive having dropped six straight after the Pelicans prevailed Wednesday in overtime, 120-113. The Mavericks and Jazz share a common opponent this week, as Jazz fell Monday to the Spurs, 119-97.

The Jazz organization's goals remain more focused on developing their young core than immediate playoff contention, but in dealing for forward Jaren Jackson Jr. last spring, CEO Danny Ainge moved beyond the rebuilding phase of angling for draft position with a trade that greatly bolstered the team's chances (and expectations) of winning now. Jackson's departure against the Grizzlies Oct. 26 with a torn MCL means that the team will turn to the stockpile of talent amassed in recent drafts, like forward Ace Bailey, guard Darryn Peterson, and point guard Keyonte George.

All three of those players seem to have bright futures, but it is Lewisville's George who has emerged as the most NBA-ready player as of this writing. The big guard hit some big shots against New Orleans Wednesday, icing a jumper that seemed to have won it before replays revealed that the ball left his hands a split second late, then knocking down the first six points of overtime coming off high screens from center Lauri Markkanen. Though the Jazz got blown out by the Spurs Monday, the previous matchup of these teams Oct. 28, a 117-111 OT Spurs win, provided some insight as to how this Jazz team can be dangerous. Playing in their first game since the Jackson injury, George keyed a Utah comeback with a drive and layup that tied it in the final minute, and guard Brice Sensabaugh made the three that set up George's heroics, plus another three in overtime.

For the second time in a week the Mavericks face an electric scoring guard from the 2026 draft class. Sacramento's Darius Acuff's 10 of 21 performance against Dallas Monday improved his season shooting percentage to .406. Utah's Peterson, shooting 34% on the season, has shown flashes of his handle and shot creating ability, but at times has looked like a rookie trying to find his role in the offense.

Markkanen, the Jazz' other veteran big man who appears ready to win now, has been tested in Jackson's absence, chasing a 2-11 three-point shooting performance against Portland with an excellent 4-7 effort from deep against the Spurs. After disappearing for much of the second half against the Pelicans, Markkanen emerged in the final two minutes of regulation to drill a three that brought the Jazz to within one and a pair of foul shots that pushed them in front a possession later. Shouldering the load as Utah's primary frontcourt threat (starting center Jusuf Nurkic is out with a toe injury) has exposed Markkanen's strengths and flaws alike. Wednesday the Jazz produced their second 40-point quarter of the season in the third, as Markkanen and reserve center Mohamed Bamba pushed and stretched a small Pelicans lineup around the floor and the Jazz attacked the rim relentlessly. But when New Orleans went big late, Zion Williamson, Derik Queen, and Saddiq Bey all got the shots they needed against Markkanen.

Some of the Mavericks' most effective stretches against the Spurs came with PJ Washington Jr., Morez Johnson Jr., and Caleb Martin taking turns as the biggest Mavs on the floor, as Dallas' small lineup cut into the Spurs' lead even after Victor Webanyama re-entered the game. If coach Dusty May employs a similar strategy against Utah, Markkanen and Bamba will have to cover a lot of ground to keep up.

Friday's game will be the Mavericks' second of the group stage of the in-season tournament and the Jazz' first. Dallas beat Houston Friday, 116-111, to notch a 1-0 record in the group stage and a +5 point differential. Dallas trails Denver for first place in West group A, as the Nuggets' +7 point differential after their 127-120 win against Phoenix Friday gave them the tiebreaker.

Mavericks guard Walter Clayton Jr. appeared in 45 games for the Jazz last season with averages of 6.8 points and 5.5 assists before being included in the Feb. 3 trade with Memphis that brought Jaren Jackson Jr. to Utah. Jazz guard Josh Green, a Maverick fan favorite from 2020-24, comes off the bench for 3.0 points per game, and is still making things happen with hard cuts and hustle plays.

#2730. Ravens were down to their third QB and had a predictably ugly performance in blowout loss to Jaguars

It was sad watching the Baltimore Ravens on Thursday night.

The Ravens were a Super Bowl contender not long ago. Many thought they could bounce back from a bad year and be a top team again this season. It's a reason they were scheduled for a prime-time game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 9. But Lamar Jackson got hurt early this season, then got hurt again last Sunday, and Tyler Huntley got hurt too.

That left the Ravens to play undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, their third quarterback, on Thursday night. He played through an injured ankle and ended up having to deal with a rainstorm most of the night. He was the Ravens' only option left, and the results were predictable. The Jaguars caught the Ravens at the right time and had an easy night in a 33-10 win. The Ravens finished with 57 yards passing.

The Ravens (4-5) have decisions to make before the trade deadline. They are reportedly on the verge of dealing for Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, and while that will make them a functional offense, it's unlikely Brissett saves the season. Jackson might return from a right thumb injury but that's no guarantee, and the Ravens might be well out of the race by the time he is healed anyway.

Thursday night was an uncompetitive, bad game. The Jaguars (6-2) are clearly one of the best teams in the NFL this season, but practically any team would have defeated Baltimore on Thursday night. There wasn't anything the Ravens or Fagnano could do, no matter how many tricks they had in the game plan. It was an unwinnable situation, which might be the case for the rest of their season too.

The Ravens opened in a wildcat formation with Derrick Henry getting the first snap of the game at quarterback. There were more wildcat plays, extra linemen and any other tricks the Ravens could figure out. Henry even had a pass completion on the first drive.

No amount of trickery was saving the Ravens. The Jaguars are a good team with a strong defense and Baltimore couldn't move the ball. The rain didn't help. Baltimore had 27 yards passing in the first half. Its longest completion was 7 yards and its longest play was 9 yards in the first two quarters.

Baltimore was trying to stay in it until Jacksonville hit a big play late in the half. Against a blitz, Trevor Lawrence found Parker Washington downfield, and he was in the clear to run for a 50-yard touchdown. Lawrence had 197 passing yards in the first half, more than six times what his counterpart Fagnano had at halftime.

Washington's touchdown made the score 17-3. It's hard to count an NFL team out with a half to go, but it was hard to believe Baltimore would score 14 more points, much less outscore Jacksonville by 14.

Coming out of halftime, Ravens head coach Jesse Minter optimistically told Amazon Prime Video he wanted to see his offense score on the first drive and see what happened after that. The Ravens threw an interception on the first drive.

The Ravens were trailing 20-3 when they got a break, as Travis Hunter fumbled and Baltimore recovered near midfield. But the Ravens couldn't get a first down, and on fourth-and-inches tight end Mark Andrews, lined up for what looked like a tush push, fumbled the snap. It looked like he was going to turn and hand it off but it didn't matter because he couldn't hold onto the ball.

It was that kind of night. The Jaguars caused some of those issues too. Their defense is very good, and the offense is capable of putting up a lot of points if there's not a downpour of rain. They have a good chance of making a deep playoff run.

The same could have been said about the Ravens before Jackson's latest injury. Brissett will be an upgrade over what we saw against the Jaguars, but there was a reason he was demoted to third string by Arizona this week and then was available in a trade. The Ravens' season probably isn't going anywhere. Things could look even worse in Baltimore by Tuesday's trade deadline.

Per ESPN's Jamison Hensley, this is the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history they've lost three straight games by at least 20 points. They at least get a long rest before "Monday Night Football" against the Los Angeles Chargers next week, at which point trade acquisition Jacoby Brissett should be ready to go.

Somehow, the game wasn't as close as the score made it look. The Jaguars finish off a beatdown of a Ravens team starting its last resort at quarterback.

Trevor Lawrence had a few moments of brilliance, and that was all Jacksonville needed to make this game one-sided from the start.

Joe Fagnano isn't thriving, but he isn't quitting either. He scrambles and makes a guy miss to convert a 3rd-and-9.

That 3-yard run brings Justice Hill up to 77 on the night. He got 65 of those on a single run, but that's still enough to break a 24-game streak of the Jaguars defense not allowing a 75-yard rusher, assuming he doesn't lose any of those yards.

A Raven somehow broke that streak in this game, and it wasn't Derrick Henry.

And now a 3-and-out for the Jaguars, who punt it to the Ravens' 13-yard line.

Justice Hill gets a little dignity back with a 65-yard touchdown run. That at least perked up what remains of the crowd.

Chris Rodriguez Jr. punches it in from two yards out on a direct snap. 7:26 to go in a classic "sim to end" game.

The Ravens' last three drives have ended in turnovers while gaining nine yards total. This is some impressively awful football.

Looks like the Ravens are about to lose a fumble on the kickoff return. The Jaguars challenge after LeJohntay Wester was ruled down by contact and replay makes it look like they will win it.

The Jaguars have gained 50 yards total since halftime. That's all they've needed to put this game well out of reach with 11:52 remaining.

Jourdan Lewis picks off Joe Fagnano at the Baltimore 23 and the Jaguars are probably about to score again.

Fagnano is 9-for-17 for 46 yards, 0 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. Expectations were low tonight and, well, the offense has acted accordingly.

Cam Little is good from 47 after the drive stalls out. Carry on.

The good news for the Ravens is Kyle Hamilton is on the sideline and doesn't seem to be in any distress. So that might just be a "why would we risk this" type of ruling out.

#2727. Carmelo and La La Anthony reach divorce settlement 9 years after first splitting

Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony (née Vázquez) reportedly have reached a settlement agreement after almost a decade-long split.

Although terms of the separation are confidential, there was a pending judgment of divorce that needed approval from the New York County Supreme Court as of Wednesday, according to People.

Once the former MTV VJ and the NBA star receive the official imprint from a judge, they'll be newly minted singles.

La La filed for divorce from the NBA star back in 2021, citing irreconcilable differences, according to TMZ, which first reported on the settlement Wednesday.

The couple began dating in 2003 after being introduced through a mutual friend, DJ Clue. They became engaged on Christmas Day 2004 and three years later welcomed their son, Kiyan Anthony, now a 19-year-old sophomore at Syracuse University, where he is playing college basketball.

The two tied the knot in July 2010 in a New York ceremony with hundreds of guests, among them sports and entertainment stars including LeBron James, Spike Lee, Serena Williams, Ciara, Kim Kardashian and Ludacris, The Times reported.

Reports of their separation surfaced in April 2017, and by August of that year, Carmelo had welcomed a daughter with ex Mia Burks.

Although the Anthonys reconciled in late 2018, they ultimately called it quits in July 2019, according to People.

La La was already using a divorce label despite it not yet being official.

In a 2022 episode of Alex Cooper's "Call Her Daddy" podcast, La La opened up about her split from Carmelo, saying that there were still difficult moments, especially regarding the co-parenting of Kiyan.

"I learned how strong I am," she said when asked about what she'd learned from the divorce. "You just find yourself getting stronger and stronger. What do they say? Like you don't know how strong you are until being strong is your only option."

La La also shared that the demise of their marriage began around the time that Carmelo was traded from the Denver Nuggets to the New York Knicks in 2011.

At the time of the 2022 interview, she shared that her perspective on love had changed. "I just don't know if it's in the cards for me," she said on the podcast.

However, in a more recent October interview on "The Jennifer Hudson Show," she revealed she was "open" to dating and that this was her "season of being open" for someone who is confident and adventurous.

As for the NBA Hall of Famer, he was rumored to be dating Racquel Smith, the widow of former NFL defensive end Will Smith. The two were seen together in June.

#2724. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2723. Ravens discussion: instant reactions to Week 9 loss to Jaguars

The Baltimore Ravens came into their Thursday night matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars with low expectations – which they met. Undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano managed just 60 passing yards on a clearly-injured ankle, and the Ravens' defense allowed far too many explosive plays through the air. Here are Baltimore Beatdown's instant reactions to the 33-10 defeat:

I am going to take a far more charitable tack towards this loss than my colleagues. It went, more or less, exactly as I expected. The Ravens showed up early and looked, in brief spurts, like they could hang around in the game, but it was clearly a mirage. Declan Doyle's creativity was limited by Joe Fagnano's apparently inability to plant and throw off his ailing right ankle, especially behind a porous offensive line that could not hold the Jaguars' defensive front. Baltimore's defense was not going to miraculously turn around in less than a week, especially against one of the NFL's top offensive minds in Liam Coen. That's a perfect recipe for a blowout, especially with a home crowd that was (understandably) ready to check out early. The offense can flush this one and move on with Jacoby Brissett, but the defense under Jesse Minter and Anthony Weaver has been bad. Shockingly bad. The unit needs a major personnel overhaul this offseason.

I don't even know what to say or do at this point. We all knew this game had the potential to get ugly but I don't think any of us had pictured exactly this ugly. I dont know where the Ravens go for here but there's still eight more games to go. This product was unwatchable so as much as I hate investing more capital into the 2026 Ravens, the Jacoby Brissett trade seems necessary, just for the fact so the weapons on the outside don't look as miserable as they did tonight. I don't think I saw Zay Flowers smile once.

At lot of questions need to be answered, but that won't happen till this offseason. Until then, we trudge on and survive. Hopefully they'll sell a few pieces at the deadline and kickstart the process.

I've lived through some dark times as a fan of this team, but it's been a while since I've felt this way. Maybe since the Super Bowl hangover when they lost a lot of pieces of the title team, but this iteration hints at some dark days to come with all of the bloated contracts and none of the payoff of having won a title. They should absolutely sell at the deadline. They need a hard reset on the roster and whatever it takes to shift the broken mentality of this group, especially that defense.

My thoughts are with Jacoby Brissett. I just hope he goes out there and has some fun playing ball.

Rock bottom. Everything that could have gone wrong did. The players plaguing the team with mistakes week after week kept doing so. The few standout players this year struggled today, adding insult to injury. The offense was putrid. Declan Doyle didn't trust Joey Fagnano to push the ball at all, which is an even bigger statement on the state of a fully healthy offensive line. The defense continued to show a lack of effort. I wonder how Marlon Humphrey will blame the fans this time. Jacoby Brissett is definitely better than Fagnano, but not enough to make up for this woefully underperforming roster. Jacksonville is a great team, but they didn't need to look like one to win convincingly tonight. Hopefully, the Ravens can show up for the occasion under the lights in Week 10 against the worst team in the league. But, man, I am struggling to find any reason to be excited for that game.

There really isn't too much to say about this team right now. This simply isn't a good enough roster, especially without Lamar Jackson at quarterback. An undrafted rookie quarterback never had a chance in this situation on a short week, dealing with an ankle injury on top of everything else. Too many of the Ravens' top-paid players and veterans continue to underperform, whether it's Marlon Humphrey giving up a massive completion on the first drive, Mark Andrews fumbling a direct snap on fourth down or he and Ronnie Stanley both having their weekly false starts. Baltimore just needs to get through this season and gut this roster in the offseason. Jackson potentially returning at some point this season almost feels pointless, because even he would have a hard time putting this team over the hump if they somehow, against all odds, made a playoff push. I want to give Jesse Minter a full offseason to try and get his guys in the building to rebuild the defense, but I would be lying if I didn't admit that he has been extremely disappointing so far.

#2719. Ravens' Kyle Hamilton exits Jaguars game with hip injury

The Baltimore Ravens were getting blown out by the Jacksonville Jaguars, whose defense was slowly suffocating an offense led by a third-string, undrafted rookie quarterback. And then things got worse.

Ravens All-Pro safety Kyle Hamilton was ruled out for the rest of the game, a 33-10 Jaguars win, with a hip injury in the third quarter. He was later seen standing on the sideline, which could be a hopeful sign that the Ravens didn't lose their best defensive player only a few days after losing Lamar Jackson.

It's unclear when exactly Hamilton sustained the injury, but Jonas Shaffer of the Baltimore Banner speculated it could have been on a play where he dove for an errant pass by Trevor Lawrence.

Ravens head coach Jesse Minter didn't have much of an update after the game, telling reporters the team should learn more later:

"Anytime someone leaves the game, you're concerned. Don't know much about it yet, [we'll] get more information tonight and tomorrow and see where that's at."

Hamilton in his fifth season and has earned All-Pro honors in each of the past three years, first-team in 2023 and 2025 and second-team in 2024. His athleticism, versatility and football IQ make him arguably the most valuable part of the Ravens defense.

A significant injury would also be a first for Hamilton in his NFL career, as he played at least 15 games in each of his first four seasons.
